text:
**The Joined-Up Line: Why Primary Schools Should Keep Teaching Cursive**

Every few years, someone declares handwriting dead. The keyboard has won, the argument goes, so why spend precious classroom hours teaching seven-year-olds to loop an "l" and join it to an "e"? It is a tidy argument. It is also wrong. Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, and they should teach it well, not as a nostalgic ritual but because it does real work for children's reading, thinking and independence.

Start with what the critics get right, because they get some of it right. Adults rarely write by hand for long stretches. Most of us scribble shopping lists, sign for parcels, and fill in the odd form. Typing is a vital skill, and no child should leave primary school unable to use a keyboard fluently. A curriculum is a zero-sum game, too, and every hour spent on letter formation is an hour not spent on fractions or fiction. If joined-up writing were merely a pretty skill, it would deserve to lose that contest.

But it is not merely pretty. Consider first what happens in a child's hand and brain when they write a letter themselves. Several studies, including work by Karin James at Indiana University, have found that children who draw letters by hand show richer activity in the brain's reading-related regions than children who type or trace the same letters. The explanation is plausible and intuitive. A typed "a" is the same press of the same key every time. A handwritten "a" must be built from a sequence of movements, and it comes out slightly different on each attempt. That variability seems to help the brain learn that many different-looking marks all count as the same letter. For a child learning to read, that is precisely the insight needed.

None of this proves that joined writing, specifically, beats printing. Fair enough. The evidence for cursive over print is thinner than its defenders sometimes claim, and I would be wary of anyone who says otherwise. So the case has to rest on something other than neuroscience alone. It rests on fluency, on spelling, and on equity.

Take fluency first. Printed letters are written one at a time, with the pen lifting off the page after every stroke. Each lift is a small break in the flow of thought. A joined script, taught properly, lets the hand travel across a whole word in one movement. The child stops thinking about the letters and starts thinking about the sentence. This matters enormously in the years between seven and eleven, when children are being asked to write longer and more complicated pieces for the first time. A child who labours over each letter has less attention left for vocabulary, structure and meaning. Handwriting that has become automatic frees the mind for composition, and several researchers, notably Steve Graham in the United States, have found that fluent handwriting predicts the quality and length of children's writing. The link is strong. It is not a small effect.

Joined writing also helps with spelling, and this is an underrated point. When a child writes "ing" or "tion" as one continuous movement, the hand learns the pattern as a unit. The movement becomes a kind of muscle memory for the word's shape. Teachers who use joined scripts from an early age often report that common letter strings stick faster, and that children are less prone to the reversals and odd letter orders that plague early writers. I would not overstate it. But the mechanism is sensible, and it costs nothing extra: if children must learn a handwriting style anyway, why not choose the one that builds in the rhythm of English spelling?

Then there is the matter of speed. By the end of primary school, children face timed assessments, note-taking, and, soon enough, secondary school exams written by hand. A child who prints can write only so fast before their letters fall apart. A child with a fluent joined hand can keep going. This is not an argument about tradition. It is a practical point about who gets to show what they know when the clock is running. Slow, effortful handwriting quietly penalises children whose ideas outrun their pens, and those are often the children who most need a break.

Which brings me to equity, and to what I think is the strongest reason of all. Typing is only a replacement for handwriting if every child has a keyboard. They do not. Some homes have a laptop for every member of the family. Others have a single shared phone. A school that drops handwriting instruction in favour of keyboards is making a bet that the technology will be there, working, charged, and available in every lesson and every exam. That bet fails exactly where children are already most disadvantaged. Pen and paper are cheap, robust and universal. Teaching a fast, legible, comfortable hand gives every child, whatever their circumstances, a tool that needs no battery and no wifi. Abandoning that is not progress. It is a quiet transfer of advantage to the children who already have the most.

There is a further point about dyslexia and other learning differences, one where the evidence is mixed but the practical experience of many teachers is consistent. Some specialists recommend a joined, flowing script for children with dyslexia, because the continuous movement reduces the confusion between letters such as "b" and "d" that look alike when printed as separate shapes. Others find that it makes no difference, or that a simplified print style suits particular children better. The sensible conclusion is not that cursive is a cure. It is that a school with a settled handwriting policy, taught explicitly and early, can spot struggling children sooner and help them, whereas a school that has let handwriting wither has few tools left to offer.

The strongest objection is the one about time. Teaching handwriting properly is not a matter of handing out worksheets. It takes short, regular, supervised practice, ideally ten or fifteen minutes a few times a week, with a teacher who watches how pencils are held and how letters are started. That is a real cost. I do not dismiss it. But set it against the cost of the alternative: children who reach secondary school with a slow, painful, illegible scrawl that no one ever taught them to improve. Many teachers know these pupils. They are bright, they have things to say, and their handwriting holds them back for years. Prevention is cheaper than cure.

Here, then, is what I would actually propose. Teach print first, in the reception year, because small children need simple shapes. Introduce joins early, from about age six or seven, once letter formation is secure. Keep the style plain: the looping, ornate scripts of the Victorian copybook are not required, and a simple, mostly unjoined-at-the-capitals hand is perfectly serviceable. Insist on legibility and fluency rather than beauty. Teach keyboarding alongside, from about age eight or nine, so that children leave primary school competent at both. The two skills are partners, not rivals.

What I would resist is the idea that this is an either-or choice, forced on schools by the march of technology. It is not. Children can and should learn to type. They should also learn to write by hand, and to do it quickly, clearly and without strain. A joined script is the most natural way to achieve that. It gives the hand a rhythm, the speller a pattern, and the writer a freedom to think ahead of the pen.

Handwriting will not vanish because we stop teaching it, any more than arithmetic vanished when calculators arrived. It will simply become something that some children learn well, at home or at private lessons, and others never learn at all. We have seen how that story ends. The children left behind are never the ones with laptops.

So keep the lessons. Keep them short, keep them explicit, and keep them joined-up. The case for doing so is not sentiment. It is a plain judgement about what helps children read, spell, write and sit exams, and about who loses out if we give it up.
